query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the Cu content in the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating by about +5 at.% (relative to the equiatomic baseline) will enhance diffusion‐induced Cu segregation at high temperatures, thereby accelerating the formation of a continuous protective oxide and/or nanocrystalline layer during sliding. This microstructural evolution mediates reduced wear depth and less severe microscopic plastic deformation. Conversely, a -5 at.% reduction in Cu should delay or hinder such beneficial oxide/nanostructure formation, resulting in increased wear and enhanced microscopic deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating deposited on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Systematically adjust the Cu concentration by ±5 at.% relative to the equiatomic baseline.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding regime where elevated temperatures enable significant diffusion, oxidation, and nanocrystallization (e.g., operating conditions where both diffusion kinetics and oxide formation are active).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a protective oxide (or spinel) layer and diffusion-driven nanocrystallization that refines the microstructure at the sliding interface.
generation.mechanism: A controlled increase in Cu content promotes selective Cu segregation during high-temperature exposure, which in turn accelerates oxidation kinetics and favors the formation of a continuous, protective oxide or nanocrystalline phase at the contact surfaces. This protective layer restricts wear and minimizes microscopic plastic deformation during sliding. A decrease in Cu would have the opposite effect by retarding these beneficial transformations.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline equiatomic coating, the +5 at.% Cu variant will exhibit lower wear rates and reduced microscopic deformation due to a more robust and continuous protective oxide/nanostructured layer; the -5 at.% Cu variant will show increased wear and higher degrees of microscopic deformation.
generation.baseline: An equiatomic FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating on a conventional metal substrate without Cu compositional modification.
generation.boundary: These predictions are expected to hold in high-temperature sliding conditions where diffusion-assisted processes and oxide formation dominate the wear and deformation behavior. The outcomes may not apply at lower temperatures where such mechanisms are inactive.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies suggest that altering elemental ratios can influence oxidation kinetics and microstructural evolution, the precise quantitative impact of a ±5 at.% Cu variation on wear resistance and deformation mechanisms remains uncertain and may be influenced by additional factors such as local temperature gradients and substrate interactions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of FeNiCrCoCu thin coatings on identical conventional metal substrates with Cu contents at equiatomic, +5 at.%, and -5 at.% levels. Subject all samples to high-temperature sliding tests using a standard tribometer. Simultaneously, perform in situ or post-test microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM, TEM, XRD) to evaluate the formation of oxide layers and any nanocrystallization at the wear surfaces.
measurements: Wear depth and wear volume measurement
Coefficient of friction during sliding tests
Characterization of surface oxide phase and nanostructure (using XRD, SEM, TEM)
Elemental mapping (e.g., via EDS) to detect Cu segregation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the +5 at.% Cu coating does not show a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and microscopic deformation (and lacks evidence of a continuous protective oxide/nanocrystalline layer) relative to the baseline, or if the -5 at.% Cu coating does not exhibit comparatively higher wear and deformation, the hypothesis that controlled Cu variation governs wear resistance via the proposed mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract WVTaTiCr x ( x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) refractory high-entropy alloy coatings were prepared on a 42-CrMo steel plate using laser cladding. The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. The addition of Cr greatly improves the hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The WVTaTiCr (Cr 1 ) exhibited superior mechanical properties, especially in terms of its exceptional hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance. This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. decision.trend: Early studies on high-entropy alloy coatings and bulk specimens under high-temperature wear conditions primarily documented macroscopic wear responses and, in subsequent work, linked these responses to microstructural changes such as oxide/spinel formation, elemental diffusion, and nanocrystallization. In the 2019 study (PMC7515071) on an AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 HEA, the formation of a high-temperature spinel phase was correlated with a decrease in wear depth, while complementary work (PMC10142552) demonstrated that varying elemental content (e.g., Cr) can influence oxide formation and phase distribution. Overall, the research sequence moved from identifying wear performance trends toward correlating these trends with microscopic phenomena, yet the specific role of controlled compositional variations in triggering such microstructural mechanisms has not yet been isolated.
decision.unsolved: How controlled adjustments—specifically, modifying the concentration of Cu within the FeNiCrCoCu HEA coating—affect the kinetics of diffusion-related segregation, the formation of a protective oxide layer, and the consequent nanocrystalline evolution that governs both wear resistance and microscopic deformation under high-temperature sliding conditions remains unaddressed.
decision.lever: Systematically vary the Cu content by ±5 at.% relative to the equiatomic baseline in the FeNiCrCoCu coating
decision.why: Previous studies have shown that oxide formation and phase evolution during high-temperature sliding are sensitive to compositional nuances. Adjusting the Cu concentration leverages the observation that selective element segregation can trigger beneficial oxide and nanocrystalline structures. This targeted compositional variation directly tests the role of Cu in governing oxidation kinetics and microstructural evolution—crucial factors for wear resistance and microscopic deformation—thus following naturally from the established trend and addressing the unresolved mechanistic question.
